item.title: I tried to build a media library that never transcodes, and the clients made that almost impossible
item.itunes:title: I tried to build a media library that never transcodes, and the clients made that almost impossible
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Transcoding sounds great on paper. I mean, why would you not want your media server to decode a video file on the fly, change its format, resolution, or bitrate, and re-encode it into a format the client device can actually play? It sounds like a feature you would actually want to use, but if you are self-hosting like me, you would go to any lengths to disable transcoding.

It comes at a massive hardware cost and can ruin the whole experience if you don't have powerful hardware running your server. I have recently been on a mission to obliterate transcoding from my media server, but the process has been an absolute minefield, and what makes it almost impossible is the clients.

The big offenders

Every client has a different requirement

You could have the most meticulously organized media library, with every file encoded to perfection, and it still wouldn't matter if the device on the other end refuses to play it. That's where the real nightmare begins. Every client has its own idea of what counts as a playable media file, and sometimes all it takes is one unsupported audio codec or subtitle track to send your server straight back into transcoding.

Take the Apple ecosystem, for example. Apple TV and iOS devices have excellent hardware, but their native media playback has strict container and codec limitations. MKV support is a headache, AV1 support depends on the hardware and software, and even HEVC can become problematic depending on how the file is packaged. Then there are ASS/SSA subtitles, which can lose their styling or require the server to burn them into the video. Congratulations, your perfectly playable video is now being transcoded because of subtitles.

Web browsers are another minefield. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all have different codec capabilities, and support often depends on the underlying operating system and hardware. HEVC compatibility is particularly inconsistent. Add TrueHD or DTS audio, and you can forget native playback. At the very least, your server has to transcode the audio, even if the video itself is perfectly compatible.

Stop ruining your Apple TV 4K's picture quality - how to fix its video settings

Play content as mastered

3
By  Samir Makwana

You would think smart TVs would be better, considering that playing media is practically their entire purpose. Unfortunately, LG webOS and Samsung Tizen bring their own problems. Underpowered SoCs, inconsistent codec support, licensing restrictions, and limitations around high-bitrate 4K playback all complicate direct play. Samsung even dropped DTS audio support years ago, which means a perfectly good video file can trigger transcoding simply because of its audio track.

And then there is Roku, which deserves a special mention for being incredibly picky about what it accepts. Codec profiles, audio formats, subtitle formats, and even the way streams are packaged can determine whether a file plays directly or gets handed back to the server for conversion. A file that works flawlessly on one device can suddenly become a transcoding job on Roku.

You either use multiple clients or disable transcoding

You need to make this choice

The frustrating part is that none of these devices fail in exactly the same way, so you can’t really build a predictable server. For example, a file that directly plays on your Apple TV might require transcoding in a browser. Or a video that works perfectly on your LG TV might run into audio compatibility issues on a Samsung. Fix one problem, and another device finds something else to complain about.

And that brings me to the fundamental problem with trying to eliminate transcoding – you're not optimizing your library for one media player. You are trying to satisfy an entire ecosystem of devices that cannot agree on what a playable media file should look like.

Unless you are willing to maintain multiple versions of the same content or restrict yourself to a very specific set of clients, achieving universal direct play becomes an exercise in chasing compatibility rather than simply enjoying your media.

Getting around the transcoding mess

It's a multi-step process

So, how do you actually get around this mess? The unfortunate reality is that you cannot expect every client to adapt to your media. If you want to eliminate transcoding, your media must bend to the lowest common denominator of your devices. And after plenty of trial and error, I have narrowed the solution down to three things.

First, standardize your file formats. MP4 is your safest bet for compatibility, although MKV works perfectly well with capable players like Infuse or Kodi. Stick to H.264 for 1080p and HEVC Main/Main 10 for 4K, as long as your clients support it. For audio, always include an AAC stereo or AC3 5.1 compatibility track, while retaining TrueHD or DTS-HD MA as a secondary track for your home theater. The goal is to give every device something it can play without involving your server.

Second, stop letting subtitles sabotage everything. You could have the perfect video and audio combination, only for an unsupported subtitle track to bring it all crashing down. ASS, SSA, and PGS subtitles can force the server to burn them into the video, triggering a full transcode. SRT is your safest option, and keeping an SRT alternative available eliminates one of the most frustrating compatibility headaches.

Finally, choose your clients wisely. Sometimes the easiest fix is to stop fighting your hardware. Devices like the Nvidia Shield TV Pro and Apple TV 4K offer far better playback capabilities than many built-in smart TV apps. On Apple devices, Infuse is particularly useful because its built-in decoders support MKV and numerous codecs that native players struggle with, reducing the need for server-side transcoding.

I thought all Blu-ray drives were the same until I found the perfect one for ripping physical media to Plex

All Blu-ray drives aren't created equal when you're backing up 4K movies for self-hosted media servers.

item.title: Getting a public IP undid a year of CGNAT workarounds I'd built to survive it
item.itunes:title: Getting a public IP undid a year of CGNAT workarounds I'd built to survive it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) in my home network was something that I didn’t get to negotiate. I found out about the limitation and started looking for a workaround. In more than a year of homelabbing, I tried many workarounds, and those worked.

But the equation flipped when I got a public IP address from my ISP recently. In the transition, many components of that CGNAT-workaround infrastructure disappeared, and some tried to hold their ground.

The stack CGNAT made me build

It worked. Then it became permanent.

The stack I am running today wasn’t carefully planned and built. My homelab started with just one service, Jellyfin. The need for remote access surfaced when I thought of using Jellyfin while I was away. And while setting up remote access, I learned that my connection was behind CGNAT. After that I started trying one workaround after another, and today the stack feels like a mountain, but it does whatever I think of.

Like most of the new homelabbers, I also started with Tailscale. It felt perfect for me. But when I shared my Jellyfin with one of my friends, and for it to work on his device, he had to install Tailscale, log in, and then open Jellyfin. The whole process started looking like an unnecessary hassle. That was when I moved all the services that were intended for public exposure to Cloudflare Tunnel. For a few months, it became a perfect setup again.

But then I came to know about Cloudflare’s policy on hosting a streaming service through their tunnel. On top of that, a few more reasons I'd been ignoring, like dependency and control, all stacked up and felt big. Then I started looking for alternatives. I came across Pangolin, a self-hostable Secure Access Service Edge based on WireGuard. I deployed it on a VPS I already rented and moved all Cloudflare Tunnel services to it.

In the meantime, I was testing several other self-hostable Tailscale alternatives as well. I hosted Headscale, and it replaced Tailscale’s cloud infrastructure. I even hosted NetBird, an open-source zero-trust networking platform built on WireGuard. In the end, I stayed with Pangolin and NetBird and eventually moved both of them to a separate new cheap VPS. I added another ISP (again under CGNAT) to help with my homelab’s uptime.

Until recently, my homelab was seamless and reliable. Both my ISPs were there to give my homelab internet access. My 8-year-old business laptop turned home server was handling the compute part. My old Synology NAS was used as bulk storage for services like Jellyfin, Immich, and Nextcloud. And a cheap VPS as a front door to my homelab. A limitation I'd treated as temporary had become a permanent design constraint.

Everything changed the moment my ISP put out an offer for a public IP address, and I took it.

Tailscale made my Jellyfin streaming secure, but 4Mbps made it actually work

Tailscale secured my Jellyfin remote streaming without exposing it to the world, but lowering playback made seeking and watching reliable.

6
By  Jeff Butts

What the public IP actually changed

One port forward later, I hit a wall I didn't build.

Because of me residing in the countryside, I have a limited number of ISPs to choose from. Whenever I asked my ISPs for a public IP, the quoted cost always made me pass on it. For context, I have a 300 Mbps primary and a 100 Mbps secondary connection. And the cost for a public IP was always more than half of my monthly connection cost. So, when my primary ISP ran an anniversary offer for a public IP at one-tenth of the monthly bill, I couldn’t resist and got one.

Once I got the IP address assigned, the first thing I thought was, “I can now access my home server directly.” But as soon as I started port forwarding on my dual-WAN ER605 gateway, I hit the first wall. The port forwarding didn’t work because the connection type was set to Dynamic on ER605, so the public IP was terminating on the ISP-provided ONT.

My first instinct was to remove the second NAT layer and move the PPPoE session to the gateway itself via bridge mode. But it didn’t establish a connection. I even tried to clone the MAC of the ONT — still nothing; mostly probably the ISP had put a restriction. Finally, after hours of experimenting, I discovered that the ISP’s ONT already exposed the DMZ and virtual servers. DMZ was already enabled, so I didn’t touch it, and I mirrored the virtual servers that I added in the ER605 earlier.

Finally, I could access the service on my homelab directly via the public IP address. The first successful access after hours of troubleshooting. Since virtual servers were working fine, I figured I should disable the DMZ. But as soon as I disabled it, the public access stopped working. I restored it, and I was able to access everything again. So it turned out DMZ was carrying the traffic, not the virtual servers.

After that, the first thing I did was deploy Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) and port forward 80/443. My workaround ended up like this: ONT DMZ -> ER605 (forward 80/443) -> home server (NPM).

But now I had all the previous stack with its recurring bill and a new public IP bill. The public IP bill was one-fifth of the VPS cost. I started thinking, if I removed the VPS altogether, I could save a good deal on the monthly bill.

I built an always‑on VPN gateway with a Raspberry Pi Zero to access my home lab from anywhere

It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

12
By  Ayush Pande

The half I kept, and the risk I took

The IP was cheap. The exposure wasn't.

When I sat down and started thinking about the VPS and its purpose, it became a tough call to eliminate it. The VPS was being used for two major roles in my homelab: public ingress and private access. Pangolin, along with CrowdSec, was handling the public access part, and NetBird was handling the private access to my admin-only services.

Removing the VPS came with both pros and cons. If I moved without it, I would save a good amount each month, but without it, I would lose certain self-hosted benefits like less dependency on third-party cloud and control over the path. But I settled midway.

I removed the VPS but kept half of what it did. The services Pangolin was fronting moved behind NPM, and instead of switching back to Tailscale, I relocated NetBird to my older VPS, which I was already renting and had enough room for NetBird.

The public IP itself was cheap, but removing the layer that came with the tunnel changed the exposure model. Previously, my home network wasn’t directly exposed to the internet. Pangolin was keeping my home network hidden, and CrowdSec was filtering the traffic. But now my ER605 has become the main gate between the LAN and the internet.

There was another important trade-off I didn’t account for until after the cutover. I previously added a second ISP for better uptime, but now that the public access via NPM is dependent on my primary ISP, if it goes down, my public services will go down as well. Private access would still be there because of NetBird, so I accepted the trade-off.

NetBird replaced Tailscale when I hit the 6-user limit, and it costs me $3 a month instead of $25

It used infrastructure I was already paying for

2
By  Ty Sherback

The problem left, the fixes stayed

CGNAT made me build a setup that I could depend on, but as soon as I got a public IP, half of that infrastructure became obsolete. A public IP came with a few trade-offs, but it solved a real problem in my setup. Now, both public availability and private access have different failure modes, and that is worth it. CGNAT built a whole stack, but it was still a workaround; whatever I now build with the public IP will be an enhancement.

But the equation flipped when I got a public IP address from my ISP recently. In the transition, many components of that CGNAT-workaround infrastructure disappeared, and some tried to hold their ground.

The stack CGNAT made me build

It worked. Then it became permanent.

The stack I am running today wasn’t carefully planned and built. My homelab started with just one service, Jellyfin. The need for remote access surfaced when I thought of using Jellyfin while I was away. And while setting up remote access, I learned that my connection was behind CGNAT. After that I started trying one workaround after another, and today the stack feels like a mountain, but it does whatever I think of.

Like most of the new homelabbers, I also started with Tailscale. It felt perfect for me. But when I shared my Jellyfin with one of my friends, and for it to work on his device, he had to install Tailscale, log in, and then open Jellyfin. The whole process started looking like an unnecessary hassle. That was when I moved all the services that were intended for public exposure to Cloudflare Tunnel. For a few months, it became a perfect setup again.

But then I came to know about Cloudflare’s policy on hosting a streaming service through their tunnel. On top of that, a few more reasons I'd been ignoring, like dependency and control, all stacked up and felt big. Then I started looking for alternatives. I came across Pangolin, a self-hostable Secure Access Service Edge based on WireGuard. I deployed it on a VPS I already rented and moved all Cloudflare Tunnel services to it.

In the meantime, I was testing several other self-hostable Tailscale alternatives as well. I hosted Headscale, and it replaced Tailscale’s cloud infrastructure. I even hosted NetBird, an open-source zero-trust networking platform built on WireGuard. In the end, I stayed with Pangolin and NetBird and eventually moved both of them to a separate new cheap VPS. I added another ISP (again under CGNAT) to help with my homelab’s uptime.

Until recently, my homelab was seamless and reliable. Both my ISPs were there to give my homelab internet access. My 8-year-old business laptop turned home server was handling the compute part. My old Synology NAS was used as bulk storage for services like Jellyfin, Immich, and Nextcloud. And a cheap VPS as a front door to my homelab. A limitation I'd treated as temporary had become a permanent design constraint.

Everything changed the moment my ISP put out an offer for a public IP address, and I took it.

Tailscale made my Jellyfin streaming secure, but 4Mbps made it actually work

Tailscale secured my Jellyfin remote streaming without exposing it to the world, but lowering playback made seeking and watching reliable.

6
By  Jeff Butts

What the public IP actually changed

One port forward later, I hit a wall I didn't build.

Because of me residing in the countryside, I have a limited number of ISPs to choose from. Whenever I asked my ISPs for a public IP, the quoted cost always made me pass on it. For context, I have a 300 Mbps primary and a 100 Mbps secondary connection. And the cost for a public IP was always more than half of my monthly connection cost. So, when my primary ISP ran an anniversary offer for a public IP at one-tenth of the monthly bill, I couldn’t resist and got one.

Once I got the IP address assigned, the first thing I thought was, “I can now access my home server directly.” But as soon as I started port forwarding on my dual-WAN ER605 gateway, I hit the first wall. The port forwarding didn’t work because the connection type was set to Dynamic on ER605, so the public IP was terminating on the ISP-provided ONT.

My first instinct was to remove the second NAT layer and move the PPPoE session to the gateway itself via bridge mode. But it didn’t establish a connection. I even tried to clone the MAC of the ONT — still nothing; mostly probably the ISP had put a restriction. Finally, after hours of experimenting, I discovered that the ISP’s ONT already exposed the DMZ and virtual servers. DMZ was already enabled, so I didn’t touch it, and I mirrored the virtual servers that I added in the ER605 earlier.

Finally, I could access the service on my homelab directly via the public IP address. The first successful access after hours of troubleshooting. Since virtual servers were working fine, I figured I should disable the DMZ. But as soon as I disabled it, the public access stopped working. I restored it, and I was able to access everything again. So it turned out DMZ was carrying the traffic, not the virtual servers.

After that, the first thing I did was deploy Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) and port forward 80/443. My workaround ended up like this: ONT DMZ -> ER605 (forward 80/443) -> home server (NPM).

But now I had all the previous stack with its recurring bill and a new public IP bill. The public IP bill was one-fifth of the VPS cost. I started thinking, if I removed the VPS altogether, I could save a good deal on the monthly bill.

I built an always‑on VPN gateway with a Raspberry Pi Zero to access my home lab from anywhere

It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

12
By  Ayush Pande

The half I kept, and the risk I took

The IP was cheap. The exposure wasn't.

When I sat down and started thinking about the VPS and its purpose, it became a tough call to eliminate it. The VPS was being used for two major roles in my homelab: public ingress and private access. Pangolin, along with CrowdSec, was handling the public access part, and NetBird was handling the private access to my admin-only services.

Removing the VPS came with both pros and cons. If I moved without it, I would save a good amount each month, but without it, I would lose certain self-hosted benefits like less dependency on third-party cloud and control over the path. But I settled midway.

I removed the VPS but kept half of what it did. The services Pangolin was fronting moved behind NPM, and instead of switching back to Tailscale, I relocated NetBird to my older VPS, which I was already renting and had enough room for NetBird.

The public IP itself was cheap, but removing the layer that came with the tunnel changed the exposure model. Previously, my home network wasn’t directly exposed to the internet. Pangolin was keeping my home network hidden, and CrowdSec was filtering the traffic. But now my ER605 has become the main gate between the LAN and the internet.

There was another important trade-off I didn’t account for until after the cutover. I previously added a second ISP for better uptime, but now that the public access via NPM is dependent on my primary ISP, if it goes down, my public services will go down as well. Private access would still be there because of NetBird, so I accepted the trade-off.

NetBird replaced Tailscale when I hit the 6-user limit, and it costs me $3 a month instead of $25

It used infrastructure I was already paying for

2
By  Ty Sherback

The problem left, the fixes stayed

CGNAT made me build a setup that I could depend on, but as soon as I got a public IP, half of that infrastructure became obsolete. A public IP came with a few trade-offs, but it solved a real problem in my setup. Now, both public availability and private access have different failure modes, and that is worth it. CGNAT built a whole stack, but it was still a workaround; whatever I now build with the public IP will be an enhancement.

item.title: Dell's super-tough Pro Rugged 13 Extreme delivers great performance under any condition
item.itunes:title: Dell's super-tough Pro Rugged 13 Extreme delivers great performance under any condition
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Pro Rugged 13 Extreme: ultra-durable - 6ft drop, IP66, -20F to 145F, 1,400-nit 13.3-inch FHD, Gorilla Glass 5.
  • Up to Core Ultra 7 (16-core), 64GB RAM, and onboard NPU for local AI - powerful without sacrificing ruggedness.
  • Pro Rugged 14: lighter at 4.7 lbs, IP53 and 3ft drop rating, plus Nvidia RTX Pro 500 Blackwell GPU.

This week has been an excellent one for people who love devices that don't break in a stiff wind. We only just reported on Panasonic's Toughbook range the other day, and now Dell is showing off its own super-tough selection of "Pro Rugged" laptops, including the 13 Extreme and the 14.

The Dell Pro Rugged 13 Extreme and 14 are powerhouses you can depend on

You can choose between extreme endurance or graphical prowess

Credit: Dell

To start off, the Dell Pro Rugged 13 Extreme is designed to outlast anything a workplace can throw at it. It can withstand 6-foot drops and operate in extreme temperatures from -20°F to 145°F. It also has an IP66 rating, meaning it's dust-tight and shielded against high-pressure water jets. Sure, not many people are working while being actively jetted with water, but it does mean the Pro Rugged 13 will definitely withstand torrential downpours of rain while you work outside. Even in freezing conditions, the laptop’s enhanced cold-boot capability means it can boot up when it's -4°F on battery power alone.

Fortunately, it doesn't sacrifice power to achieve all that survivability. Under the hood, we're looking at an Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processor, which can be upgraded up to the 16-core Ultra 7 368H. It has 64GB of RAM and even has its own NPU to process on-board AI models. It also sports a 13.3-inch FHD display that can max out at 1,400 nits of brightness, and it's protected by Corning Gorilla Glass 5.

If you like your laptops to be tough but you don't need things to operate at the extremes, Dell also introduced the Pro Rugged 14. It's not quite as tough as the 13 Extreme, offering an IP53 rating for dust and splashing water and a 3-foot drop rating. However, it trades heavy-duty armor for a lighter footprint (starting at 4.7 lbs) and a huge graphics upgrade, including an Nvidia RTX Pro 500 Blackwell GPU.

Dell listened and the XPS 14 is back, baby, yeah

One of the most storied names in the game is back

By  Joe Rice-Jones

item.title: I stopped giving my files useful names, but these free apps found them anyway
item.itunes:title: I stopped giving my files useful names, but these free apps found them anyway
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I, like many others, have a bad habit of not giving my files and documents proper names when I save them. I always assume I'll be able to find them when I need them, and usually that holds true, so I've kind of stopped caring to give everything a proper name. Except I don't always remember the name of a file I need.

Because of that, I needed a system that let me find any document I need by just searching inside it, which is harder than it sounds. And thankfully, there are some apps that can do exactly that while being noticeably faster than Windows 11's built-in search.

Everything finds... almost everything

Fast and capable, with one specific limitation

It's not news at this point that Windows Search is a pretty slow and frustrating search tool, and my recommendation for a while now has been Everything. It's a search tool that tells you right away what it's capable of, and indeed, finding files with it is a breeze.

Starting with its super-fast indexing speeds and instant results, there's nothing not to love about Everything's file search, but when it comes to searching content, things are a bit different. For one thing, the content of files is not indexed by Everything. All your searches are queried when you make them, meaning results take a while longer to come back and it's a good idea to narrow down your searches per location or file format.

8 ways you can optimize Everything to easily find all your files

Optimize your file searches with Everything using advanced filters, indexing, and more to quickly locate files and enhance your workflow efficiency

2
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

That's not to say Everything does a poor job at this, though. It can still return results impressively quickly, and what's more, it can scan many kinds of files. I was able to find various file types of plain text files (such as .txt, .ps1, or .yml) and even .pdf files this way, and they were returned fairly quickly with not much I could consider a "false hit".

The major problem with Everything is that it failed to find files with Office formats, whether that was Microsoft's own .docx and .xlsx or even open standards like .odt. This makes it far less useful if these are the kinds of files you want to find.

Agent Ransack fills the void

Find what was missing

This is where Agent Ransack comes in. This is another search tool, not unlike Everything, but it's presented a bit differently, and it has an arguably more user-friendly interface. All the search tools are laid out in the UI itself without needing as many submenus, so you can get to grips with the software more easily if you're a newcomer.

Agent Ransack is available in both Lite and Pro versions (though it's the same download), and while the Pro tier unlocks some advanced searching capabilities, the Lite version already supports searching within .docx and .xlsx file types. Supposedly, the Pro version offers more accurate results, but searching for text seemed to work fine in my experience with the free version.

5 best free software for searching files on Windows

Search for files on Windows easily with these five free software tools. They also offer advanced features for instant search results.

8
By  Sammy Ekaran

Feature-wise, Agent Ransack Lite has most of the basic capabilities that Everything also offers, but its biggest downside is that multi-threaded searching is not available in the free version, and results can take a while to come in. When I was testing a search within my Documents folder, it took a long time to get me results because it was scanning a Windows 11 ISO file I had saved there. You can work around this by filtering for file types or sizes, though.

Which one should you choose?

It's not necessarily one or the other

As nice as it would be to have a single tool to search inside files on my PC, I think combining these two tools would be the ideal setup. Everything is faster and lighter overall, and it gets accurate results from searching the majority of file formats, including PDF files. On the other hand, Agent Ransack is the only one that can search inside Word and Excel files, so even though it's a little slower, it's a necessity if you work with these kinds of files.

Ultimately, if you want just one app, I'd say Agent Ransack Lite is still the best free option out there. It has great search capabilities and an accessible UI, and the fact that it can search more kinds of files makes it easily the most versatile option. You can work around its slightly lower search speed by narrowing down search locations or filtering for file types and sizes, so it cancels out its biggest disadvantage.

8 reasons to stop using Windows Search and use Everything instead

Windows search can be a drag. For a better search experience, check out Everything from Voidtools.

2
By  Brian Burgess

I would say you might even consider paying for the Pro version of Agent Ransack, but I can't see it justifying the $79 investment. At that point, it might be better to improve your own file organization.

What about Windows?

It could work, but...

It's worth acknowledging that Windows has its own built-in search tool that can search inside file contents, but as I've already mentioned, there are a few too many downsides. Windows Search is notoriously slow even when you're not searching for file contents, and if you try to work around that by indexing the entire PC, that indexing process takes a long time and it pushes your PC pretty hard. It feels sluggish compared to a program like Everything.

At the same time, while Windows can search within Word and Excel files, support for those modern formats has to be provided by an installation of Microsoft Office itself. Windows alone can't filter the content of .docx formats, and alternative Office suites like OnlyOffice can't provide those search capabilities to Windows, either. It's not an ideal setup.

I stopped using Windows Search after finding Microsoft's better launcher

But you need PowerToys for it.

By  Hamlin Rozario

Finding files made easy

I was surprised to find out that Agent Ransack has been around since 2000, but after finding it, I can see why it remains a viable option today. If you want to search inside files across your entire PC, it's still a very strong offering, even in the free versions, making it an easy recommendation if you struggle to remember where your documents ended up.

item.title: Zelda: The Wind Waker finally has the native PC port fans waited decades for, complete with 120fps support
item.itunes:title: Zelda: The Wind Waker finally has the native PC port fans waited decades for, complete with 120fps support
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Unofficial Wind Waker Recomp runs natively on Windows, macOS, and iPhone/iPad with Direct3D12/Metal, 60/120fps.
  • Save states, widescreen, touch/mouse/keyboard/controller support, wall climbing, and support for the Dolphin HD texture pack.
  • Made with AI help, it emulates GameCube hardware (no JIT), adds 4x rendering and HD fixes; needs your GameCube copy.

The world of retro video game recompilations is getting increasingly wild.

The latest release is a static recompilation of The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker that runs natively on Windows, Mac, iPhone, and iPad. The very unofficial port of the GameCube classic features Direct3D 12 and Metal rendering, 60fps/120fps, widescreen, save states, and wall climbing. It also supports touch controls, mouse and keyboard, and controller input.

Elliottate, the developer behind the project, says that Wind Waker Recomp is a fork of Bluewake, an iPhone and iPad Zelda: The Wind Waker static recompilation effort from Chrissotraidis (Chris Sotraidis). Like most recomps, you need your own legally obtained copy of The Wind Waker for the GameCube to play the port. As always, it's pretty easy to find disc images online if you know where to look.

It's also worth noting that both BlueWake and Wind Waker Recomp have been developed with substantial AI assistance for code, testing, documentation, and debugging. On Windows, the classic Zelda titles run on x86-64, while the Mac, iPhone, and iPad versions are arm64.

All of Wind Waker HD's key improvements are part of Wind Waker Recomp

HD texture packs are compatible with the recompilation, too

Elliottate adds that Wind Waker Recomp runs with a compatibility runtime for the GameCube's hardware that includes memory, timing, disc and memory card, controllers, DSP audio, and graphics through Direct3D 12 on Windows and Metal on Apple devices. Since nothing is compiled while the game is being played, JIT isn't necessary.

Additional quality-of-life upgrades include compatibility with Dolphin-format HD texture packs like GZLE01, and the ability to render the game at 4x the GameCube's 480 lines. Wind Waker also includes Wind Waker HD improvements like Swift Sail, faster text and climbing, and more. The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker HD was released on the Wii U in 2013, but so far, Nintendo hasn't brought the excellent remaster to the Switch 2.

As far as retro Zelda titles go, Zelda: The Wind Waker has aged remarkably well despite being 24 years old, thanks to its beautiful, cartoony art style, which was actually very controversial when the game first released for the GameCube in 2003.

If you want to try out Wind Waker Recomp for yourself, you can find the game at this link (you'll also need to get your hands on a disc image). In other recompilation-related news, a browser-based port of Halo: Combat Evolved recently dropped, featuring 128-player multiplayer.

You can now play the original Halo for free in your browser with 128-player multiplayer

Activision may have taken over the Halo series, but at least you can play the OG game in a browser now.

item.title: I finally understand why old Kindles have sharper text than new ones, and it's not just nostalgia
item.itunes:title: I finally understand why old Kindles have sharper text than new ones, and it's not just nostalgia
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've used more than one Kindle e-reader over the years, it's easy to see the upgrades. Larger screens, higher contrast, adjustable warm lighting, longer battery life, and faster page turns make the newer Kindles objectively better than the older ones. That said, I still feel that older Kindle models (before Kindle Paperwhite) somehow looked sharper than the ones Amazon sells now. And I found that I'm not remembering it wrong.

The engineering behind the newer Kindles has changed substantially over the last decade and a half. More advanced display technology, front lighting, and laminated screens have made them superior to older displays, but they also make them look less lifelike. Older Kindles can feel limited in features, but their less advanced displays can look sharper in many cases.

I’m sticking with my older Kindle Paperwhite because color E Ink still isn't great

Monochrome E Ink reigns for reading

By  Samir Makwana

Older Kindle screens had fewer layers

Light diffusion reduces contrast and sharpness on newer models

Your latest Kindle Paperwhite has all the bells and whistles that make it the "best e-reader" on the market. A sensitive touchscreen and an advanced warm frontlight definitely make the reading experience more comfortable. However, the digitizer grid powering the touch-sensitive display or the frontlight layer over the E Ink screen can also diffuse the light slightly, reducing the perceived sharpness of the text on screen.

These extra waterproofing and anti-glare layers on newer models make them better than older ones, but they also come in the way of a closer connection with the paperlike E Ink display. Older Kindles, especially the ones preceding the Kindle Paperwhite, still feel sharper due to a lot less processing sitting between the screen and your eyes.

I transformed my Kindle into an e-ink Game Boy, and now I can't put it down

My hacked Kindle runs Game Boy games better than any handheld I own

2
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Built-in lighting sometimes makes newer models look less lifelike

The raw, non-lit older Kindles had it better

  • Credit:  
  • Credit: 
  • Credit:  
  • Credit: 

Older Kindles, such as the Kindle 4th Gen, didn't feature any built-in lighting. You had to rely on ambient light or a light source to read the E Ink display. This mimicked the experience of reading a real book. Later models, starting with the Kindle Paperwhite in 2012, introduced a front-lit display that illuminated the screen from below instead of from behind.

Built-in lighting made nighttime reading easier, but it also introduced a problem. Even with the frontlight turned completely off, some Kindles appeared hazy or washed out in certain conditions. Older, non-lit screens lacked the refractive light guide layer, relying on ambient light reflecting the E Ink display directly. This made the screen more tactile, thanks to the "hazy" effect being absent.

Users who've never used pre-2012 Kindles may not even find anything wrong with their readers. It's only when you've used old and new models that you can recognize the difference.

5 reasons E Ink displays might be the next big thing for PC setups

Your eye health is important and E Ink might just be the answer.

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Modern laminated screens can make text look slightly softer

You win some, you lose some

Credit: 

If you've used an older Kindle, the recessed display (sitting slightly lower than the bezel) makes the text look sharper. It felt closer to reading real ink on physical paper. Newer models use a seamless glass or plastic display sitting flush with the bezel. While the continuous screen makes cleaning and turning pages easier, it can introduce microscopic refractions, making text appear softer.

Anti-reflective coatings on newer Kindle Paperwhite models mitigate this problem to a great extent, but it's still there, giving older models yet another win. Of course, I'm not advocating you hunt for older, discontinued Kindles. However, if you, too, remember those older models looking sharper than the newer ones, you now know why.

I turned my Kindle into 4 things Amazon never intended, and now it's the most useful device on my desk

A jailbreak opened it up for several practical uses.

1
By  Samir Makwana

Nostalgia clouds your memory, but I'm not wrong on this one

Newer isn't always better, at least not in every way. Amazon's latest Kindles are superior to older models in almost every department, but the developments come with a loss in text sharpness. Extra layers on top of the E Ink layer, built-in lighting, and a laminated display come together to make a highly advanced screen, but it loses something in terms of the rawness of the display.

item.title: Here's what makes Home Assistant work so well in my smart home (and it's not the army of Zigbee sensors)
item.itunes:title: Here's what makes Home Assistant work so well in my smart home (and it's not the army of Zigbee sensors)
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Home Assistant works really well, almost too well, considering how capable this smart home platform is for the price. You can configure it to control a few smart bulbs and call it a day, or throw in a robot vacuum cleaner, smart appliances, IP cameras, energy monitoring, music playback, and more. It's not the easiest to work with, however, and there are plenty of guides available for budding smart home beginners to spend hours reading through to perfect their Home Assistant setup. This is what makes mine work so well; I shield the rest of the household from having to learn it.

And that's when Home Assistant can become incredibly powerful for the home. As long as someone understands the underlying complexities, others in the household can reap the benefits without spending any time learning the ropes.

Home Assistant isn't designed for everyone

Although recent updates are helping address this

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

The learning curve for Home Assistant is fairly steep. There are integrations, apps, YAML, network configurations, and dashboards to contend with. It's not quite deploy-and-use, as most people would prefer a smart home hub to be. This is why you'll often find households rely on prebuilt all-in-one solutions like Amazon Echo and Apple HomePod. It's best when only one chef is in the kitchen. Should multiple people get involved, you can risk having misconfigured automations and conflicting changes.

I couldn't imagine having to collaborate with someone to maintain the smart home. Home Assistant works flawlessly because I'm a sucker when it comes to perfecting everything I do. If I start to change something on the platform, I have to keep going until it's the best I can make it. While this does mean that I became the go-to person for all things that can go wrong with the smart home, it's countered by the fact that I already understand every part of the Home Assistant installation. I wrote every script and configured each automation.

My spouse, house guests, and visiting friends don't need to know how automations work. They don't even need to interact with the platform as a whole. We have a single NSPanel Pro Gen2 from Sonoff in the conservatory, acting as a means to control local lighting and view some other data, but unless one has access to the app, everything just ticks along nicely, and that's what makes the smart home truly user-friendly for everyone, regardless of how tech-savvy they happen to be.

Depending on what someone wants to do with our smart home setup, controls can be as simple as toggling a single switch to activate a light fixture or as complex as changing the mode of our DIY alarm system.

Building a local smart home is easy until you try to replace the speaker

I replaced everything with local-only hardware, but this was the most difficult.

4
By  Rich Edmonds

Newer Home Assistant versions are better

We've covered more recent versions of Home Assistant at great length here at XDA. With each passing release, we're seeing the platform become easier to use, whether it's configuring dashboards for different devices or creating complex automations that take inputs from various sensors and achieve something that would take a couple of seconds to carry out manually. That's the goal of any smart home: to make your life (and everyone else's) easier.

But no matter how easy the developers eventually make Home Assistant to administrate, there's a sizable difference between maintaining a smart home and using one. It's the same as a router (and wider local network), boiler, and central heating. These are things that usually just work with very little maintenance, and Home Assistant can be firmly placed in the same camp.

Useful automations make all the difference

These can easily transform a smart home

One of the primary reasons to use something like Home Assistant, or any smart hub, is to unlock automations. These take an input condition, process it, and perform an action. Smart bulbs could respond to occupancy, time of day, or detected ambient light levels. Alarm states could change automatically when all doors are closed and locked. Heating controls could be automatically set to come on should temperatures drop to a certain level.

The last example is one we rely on at home. Using electric radiators, it's vital we maintain comfortable temperatures without drawing too much electricity from our local battery storage and the grid. Electric radiators are anything but light on power, drawing anywhere up to 2,000 watts, if not more. Even portable oil-filled radiators can be significantly improved with smart plugs. On days when temperatures outside are below a specific threshold, they can be set to come on at periods of the day for 30 minutes or so, if people are home.

If you've owned a robotic vacuum, you'll know how they can sometimes get in the way and create quite a racket, which is what makes it impressive to those around you when they're configured to only activate scheduled routes when the house is empty and the alarm system is set to away. It also means the family pet can be kept in their favorite safe space while the machine does its thing. And if one opens up Home Assistant to the wider online world, notifications can be sent through to mobile devices.

So long as people can visually see what the smart home is doing, they're less likely to question the backend stuff. Notifications, lights turning on and off, and things occurring as expected all help create the sense of the home working away without requiring human input. Just like Jellyfin, which only requires me to touch the admin panel, it works flawlessly for anyone looking to connect and stream some of our media. I even configured it at my parents' place with no issues. It just works.

For Home Assistant, I'm almost eliminating the need for a user interface to even be present.

My smart home still works without the internet, and it's all thanks to one app

Home Assistant is the best unified platfom for your smart devices.

17
By  Adam Conway

There's one drawback: tech support

Like anything you take ownership of at home when it comes to technology, there becomes an expectation that a tech support line is available 24/7. Home Assistant is no different. A light bulb not responding to toggles in the Home Assistant app becomes an inconvenience that needs addressing. Because I'm the only one with full access to the backend, it falls on me to check what's going on. That's fine when I'm at home on the laptop with five minutes to spare, but if I'm halfway around the world, it can prove challenging without direct access and availability.

Still, the positives more than make up for this single drawback. Being able to improve our home with technology, without requiring everyone to head to university for a degree in computer science, has allowed me to create something truly advanced for a traditional abode. And so long as no one notices the smart home is actually there with everything connected together, that's the best compliment to anyone who has set up Home Assistant and a few sensors.

item.itunes:summary:
Windows 11 and bloatware go hand in hand. Microsoft's prime directive in the last few years has been to push as many useless features and services on Windows users. This naturally inflates the number of startup applications, slowing down the boot process. Combined with third-party applications that accumulate over time, they can make your PC noticeably slower.

Most users limit the number of startup programs in Task Manager, and call it a day. Little do they know that the Startup apps tab in Task Manager exposes only a small subset of everything that launches on boot. For the full picture, you need Autoruns, a free utility from Microsoft that shows you everything that Task Manager doesn't.

4 Windows 11 startup apps I disabled to instantly speed up my PC

One bold move to instantly speed up an aging PC

9
By  Samarveer Singh

Task Manager doesn't show you everything

It's designed for simplicity, not thoroughness

The problem with using Task Manager alone to debloat your startup routine is that it's an incomplete tool for the job. While it does show you most applications loading during the boot process, along with the last boot time, it doesn't pull from every location. It simply scans your personal Startup folder, the common Startup folder (for all users on the machine), and the standard registry keys.

On your PC, applications can use a variety of other launch mechanisms, including Task Scheduler, deeper registry keys, Windows services, and Explorer add-ons. None of these are exposed in the Startup apps tab in Task Manager. The reason is that this tab is designed to show users the most common programs they might want to disable, not expose a complex web of every single entity that runs at boot.

Consequently, people assume that whatever they see in the Startup apps is the whole picture. And then they wonder why their PC still takes ages to reach the desktop. For total insight into your boot routine, you need to download Autoruns, a free Sysinternals tool from Microsoft.

A single Windows diagnostic tells you why your PC takes forever to shut down

Event Viewer should be your go-to source for diagnosing Windows anomalies

By  Tanveer Singh

Autoruns reveals the startup items you don't see

A more powerful view into your startup bloat

When you launch Autoruns and accept the disclaimer, it populates all the programs, processes, and services that run on boot. The "Everything" tab shows you, well, a list of literally everything that Windows loads during startup. To help you make sense of this, there are separate tabs for Logon, Scheduled Tasks, Explorer, Services, Drivers, Internet Explorer, AppInit, and Known DLLs, among others.

Unlike Task Manager, you now have a comprehensive view of your startup items, so you can take the necessary steps to improve your boot time. Autoruns reveals scheduled tasks left behind by software you uninstalled long ago, shell extensions from programs you've already deleted, or registry entries that point at missing files.

None of these anomalies are visible as a toggle in Task Manager, which leads users to believe that their system is free of startup detritus. If you're worried about disabling or deleting the wrong thing in Autoruns, you can click on the Options tab at the top, and ensure that both Hide Windows Entries and Hide Microsoft Entries are ticked. This prevents accidental deletion of important Windows and Microsoft services.

It's impossible to recommend paid Windows cleanup utilities when Windows Sysinternals does everything for free

No more CCleaner, dad

By  Samarveer Singh

Using Autoruns without breaking anything is the key

Don't go deleting everything that stinks

Once you've removed the Windows and Microsoft entries from the list, you're mostly left with unsigned and third-party software. To start your Autoruns cleanup, look for entries with "File not found" next to them. They'll be the yellow-highlighted items, whether you're in the "Everything" tab or some other tab. These entries are reliably safe to remove, since they're pointing at a file or location that no longer exists on your system.

Next, you can look at pink-highlighted entries, which indicate software items that aren't "verified" by Windows. These aren't necessarily malicious, since you can see entries like "qBittorrent" and "SignalRgb" in the images above. A common sight when running Autoruns is a slew of "File not found" entries in the "Known DLLs" tab. These can be safely ignored, since they're often 32-bit equivalents of 64-bit Windows entries, and don't always have a file location to point to.

That said, I did find a few anomalies on my system in the "Logon" and "Scheduled Tasks" tabs. In the former, the "OneDriveSetup" entry was still there after I had removed OneDrive months ago. And in the latter, I saw a notification manager task related to SanDisk Dashboard. My startup items in Task Manager did not have Dashboard enabled, but Autoruns still showed me that Windows was running a related task in the background.

I debloated Windows 11 without breaking anything, and here's what I deliberately left alone

How much do you trust the debloater you got from GitHub?

1
By  Abhinav Raj

Autoruns gives you complete control over your startup items

For a free utility, Autoruns is a pretty powerful one. It reveals everything hidden by the Startup items tab in Task Manager. Your view is no longer limited to a handful of known programs you've already enabled or disabled. Autoruns enables you to delete or disable any startup entry that points to a missing file or is linked to an unrecognized third-party application, so you can truly clean your startup bloat.
